Faced with increasing criticism regarding its handling of head injuries, FIFA, world soccer’s governing body, is expected to confirm a new policy this week that will allow referees to stop games for up to three minutes so that an injured player can be examined by a team doctor.
The new guideline will be instituted after FIFA’s executive committee affirms it with a vote during its two-day meeting this week in Zurich. UEFA, which oversees European soccer, adopted the protocol last week. It will be used for the first time in the Champions League next week.
The issue of concussions in soccer
became even more inflamed last summer at the World Cup
after several players appeared to sustain serious injuries only to continue playing. In the final, between Germany and Argentina, Christoph Kramer of Germany was knocked unconscious in a collision with an Argentine opponent but remained on the field for 14 minutes before being substituted.
It was revealed after the game, won by Germany, that Kramer had been disoriented after his collision. The match referee, Nicola Rizzoli of Italy,
told an Italian newspaper
that Kramer approached him shortly after getting to his feet to ask
whether he was playing in the World Cup final
; at that point, Rizzoli said he informed Germany’s captain, Philipp Lahm, who encouraged Germany’s coaches to replace Kramer.
In announcing its new policy on head injuries, FIFA referred to the events in Brazil as an impetus for its changes. Some people may find such a link bizarre — head injuries in sports are hardly a new issue — yet this adjustment is at least a small step in the direction of safety.
“The incidents at the World Cup have shown that the role of team doctors needs to be reinforced in order to ensure the correct management of potential cases of concussion,”
FIFA said in a statement
.

Since I spent
last month
hammering
away
at the legitimacy of White House’s promised executive action on immigration, you won’t be surprised to hear that I have a few thoughts following the news that
it’s been officially delayed
, at least until after the midterm elections but with no date certain set. Three thoughts, to be specific:
1) I didn’t dwell on the short-term politics much while I was attacking the proposal, but I’ve always been puzzled by the White House’s political calculations in this matter, and the delay — while welcome — only heightens my bafflement. Specifically, I don’t see why, if there was
any
substantial possibility of postponement or inaction, the administration wouldn’t have worked harder to manage expectations among activists, instead of having every leak and story over a period of months emphasize just
how all-in the president planned to go
, how determined he was to do it, how many millions
would probably be affected
when he did, etc. Yes, I know, it’s normal in politics to float trial balloons and wait to see how many outraged conservative columnists take potshots at them (and how many honorable liberals get uncomfortable). But Team Obama seemed to let this balloon get away from them, in a way that made postponement
much more politically painful
on the president’s left flank than it needed to be if they’d simply kept things more hedged and hypothetical. Or maybe they didn’t think they were floating a trial balloon, didn’t anticipate — even after the surge of unaccompanied minors started making headlines, since the biggest overpromising to activists came
after
the border surge, not beforehand — that unilateralism on immigration could be a political loser in a campaign fought mostly on reddish territory, and were genuinely blindsided by the complaints from Democratic Senate incumbents cited in some of
the stories explaining the delay
. Or maybe they were too enamored of a super-clever (but not really)
“gaslight-the-Republicans”
strategy and didn’t think hard enough about what they would do if the G.O.P. didn’t seem interested in actually impeaching the president or shutting the down the government. Or maybe there were just various factions in the White House pursuing varying agendas, and nobody stepped in to make people row together and think through the implications of each stroke. Whatever the explanation, right now the result looks like political malpractice: A base-depressing, opposition-rousing own goal that could have been rather easily avoided.
2) At the same time, I don’t want to overstate the sourness of the near-term politics: The same factors that made the promised action seem politically unwise (the fact that this year’s battlegrounds are light on Hispanic votes, especially) could also mitigate the downsides of disappointing activists and dampening turnout on the margins. But whatever happens in November, this kind of delay also creates a longer term problem for the White House, assuming that the president actually intends to follow through on the promised move, because explicitly saying “our unilateral action looks a little unpopular right now, so we’re going to do it after the midterm elections” substantially undercuts the already-shaky argument for this kind of move’s democratic legitimacy.
Or to quote
Ezra Klein
, usually more inclined than I to give this president the benefit of the doubt:
This is the problem with the White House’s decision — and, to some degree, the way they’ve managed this whole issue. If these deportations are a crisis that merits deeply controversial, extra-congressional action, then it’s hard to countenance a politically motivated delay. If they’re not such a crisis that immediate action is needed, then why go around Congress in the first place? … Obama [has] slammed Republicans for defying “the will of the majority of the American people who support reform.” It is hard to attack Republicans for defying the will of the majority of the American people but then delay your own immigration actions until after the election … The White House may be right that delaying the decision will reduce its short-term political cost. But it comes at the price of making the criticisms against the policy much more potent.
3) But there is another possibility, which is that Caesarism delayed will eventually become Caesarism eschewed altogether … or else that Obama will eventually do
something
unilaterally on immigration, but it will be much more modest (
a down payment on reform
, the White House can tell activists) than what’s been floated and promised these last few months. Maybe the politics will keep looking somewhat ugly, maybe Democrats up for election in purple states in 2016 will pressure Obama to keep punting — or maybe the president will actually heed
some of the criticism
of his plan and revert to a more modest conception of how presidential power should be exercised on this issue. I’m not such a cynic that I don’t believe the last scenario is impossible, and it’s a good reason for the White House’s critics to be pleased with this delay: Sure, it could be setting us up for an even balder power grab in four months, but where there’s procrastination there’s hope, and a journey away from executive overreach could begin with exactly this kind of step.

A large
study
in England has found that smokers trying to quit were substantially more likely to succeed if they used electronic cigarettes than over-the-counter therapies such as nicotine patches or gum. These results offered encouraging but not definitive evidence in the contentious debate about the risks and benefits of these increasingly popular smoking devices.
Researchers interviewed almost 6,000 smokers who had tried to quit on their own without counseling from a health professional. About a fifth of those who said they were using e-cigarettes had stopped smoking at the time of the survey, compared with about a tenth of people who had used patches and gum.
“This will not settle the e-cigarette issue by any means,” said Thomas J. Glynn, a researcher at the American Cancer Society, who was not part of the study, “but it is further evidence that, in a real-world context, e-cigarettes can be a useful, although not revolutionary, tool in helping some smokers to stop.”
The use of e-cigarettes has risen rapidly across Europe and the United States, and regulators are scrambling to figure out how to respond in the absence of hard evidence about their effects. The debate is particularly fierce in the United States, where some experts say the devices could lure children to start smoking, while others contend that they are the best hope in generations to get smokers to switch to something less dangerous than traditional cigarettes.
About 42 million Americans smoke, and some 480,000 people die every year from smoking-related illnesses, one of the United States’ leading causes of preventable death. The central question is whether e-cigarettes will cause the ranks of smokers to shrink or swell.
So far, the evidence is too thin to provide a convincing answer. The Food and Drug Administration has commissioned a broad study, but its results will not be known for years. A
clinical trial in
New Zealand
, which many researchers regard as the most reliable study to date, found that people given e-cigarettes had only a slightly better quit rate than those with patches. While the long-term health effects of e-cigarettes are unknown, many health experts believe that the concentrations of toxins in the vapor are much lower than in cigarette smoke.
The English study was not a clinical trial, the gold standard of scientific research, in which participants would have been randomly assigned to different groups: for example, one that used e-cigarettes to quit and another that used nicotine replacement therapies. But authors of the study said that they controlled for many factors, including social class, age, level of nicotine dependence and time since the attempt to quit first started. They also said the study, one of the largest to date, offered valuable insights into the real world experiences of smokers.
Prof. Robert West, director of tobacco studies at University College London and senior author of the study, which is to be published Wednesday in the journal Addiction, said that clinical trials could not answer the question most people have about whether e-cigarettes help smokers quit because the devices are changing so fast that they become obsolete before an experiment ends. What is more, he said, people who wanted e-cigarettes and found themselves put in a group that used, say, the patch, would just drop out.
“The medical model is great for cancer drugs, but it doesn’t really work for this situation because there’s nothing to stop participants in the patches group from just going out and buying an e-cigarette,” Professor West said.

He said the database used for the study was financed by Cancer Research UK, a nonprofit group; England’s Department of Health; and several large drug companies that make nicotine replacement therapy, including Pfizer, GlaxoSmithKline and Johnson & Johnson.
Professor West, an e-cigarette optimist, said that solid epidemiological evidence would not be available for at least several decades, while the need for policy decisions is now.
He calculated that more than 5,000 lives could be saved for every million smokers who switched to e-cigarettes, even if the devices carried significant health risks and people used them indefinitely after quitting real cigarettes.
“Potentially millions of lives are at stake, and our job is to help policy makers to protect those lives,” he said in an editorial that accompanied the study.
The standard recommended practice for helping people quit is a prescribed medicine such as Chantix or a combination of nicotine patch and gum together with counseling from a trained professional. But even in England, where these options are widely advertised and nearly free, the majority of smokers rely on willpower or nicotine products bought from a store, and success rates are low. The study found that the rate at which smokers quit by using e-cigarettes was similar to that for people who used prescribed nicotine therapy with brief counseling.
Stanton A. Glantz, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, said the study’s limitation was that it tried to measure the effect of e-cigarette use only among smokers who were trying hard to quit, not all smokers.
Professor West responded that the study’s goal was to find out whether e-cigarettes helped people who were trying to stop smoking. But he said data still being analyzed may yet provide clues to the broader effects on smokers generally.

My recent article offering
a more accurate way of judging campaign fund-raising
drew several responses, one from Bob Biersack, a former Federal Election Commission employee now with the Center for Responsive Politics. When journalists have needed to understand campaign finance during the past 30 years, Mr. Biersack has often supplied the answer, so his opinion is worth noting.
Mr. Biersack’s take
is that while discounting money that is spent to raise more money is a useful approach for understanding campaign finances, it might not be in every circumstance. He argues that because the Republican senators Marco Rubio of Florida and Rand Paul of Kentucky are not on the ballot this year, but are considered potential presidential candidates in 2016, direct mail appeals are important. (Mr. Rubio spends much more on this than Mr. Paul.)
“That’s key because one of the things prospective candidates must do is build ‘name recognition’ and visibility among party activists and others around the nation,” Mr. Biersack writes. “Direct mail fund-raising appeals can help with that, even if they don’t bring in large sums right away, because the mailings emphasize a potential candidate’s background and remind possible donors why the sender might be a good choice for national office.”
I think his argument makes a lot of sense. For actual or potential national campaigns, direct mail counts as a kind of campaign investment. But in state or district-level races, I think direct mail’s costs should factor into how we assess fund-raising as a measure of a candidate’s viability, since most direct mail campaigns employ a wide geographic scope. The example I used of the campaign in Florida’s 18th Congressional District in 2012 fits this idea better.

Around the Block
By
EZRA DYER
TESTED
Nissan Juke Nismo
WHAT IS IT?
A sportier edition of Nissan’s unapologetically offbeat crossover.
HOW MUCH?
$23,800 base, $25,215 as tested, including navigation package ($1,170) and center armrest ($245).
WHAT’S UNDER THE HOOD?
1.6-liter turbocharged 4-cylinder with direct injection (197 horsepower, 184 pound-feet of torque).
IS IT THIRSTY?
No. The manual-shift version (front-wheel drive only) earns an E.P.A. rating of 25 m.p.g. city and 31 m.p.g. highway.
Nissan, these days, makes two kinds of cars. There are the inoffensive high-volume machines like Sentra, Altima, Rogue and Pathfinder. And then there are the others, vehicles so keenly focused (and often eccentric) that you’d think they came from an entirely different maker. These include the Leaf, the Murano CrossCabriolet, the Cube, the GT-R and today’s subject, the Juke Nismo.
The Juke looks like the company car for Zog, Lord of the Xterra Galaxy. Which reminds me: put the Xterra in that second group, too. Most crossovers can’t risk indulging in a polarizing exterior design. But Nissan already has the Rogue to chase mainstream buyers, so the Juke can afford to get freaky.
The Juke Nismo — a quicker, more powerful Juke — presumes you’re already on board with the Juke’s styling but would like its performance enhanced by the Nissan Motorsports department, known as Nismo.
About that styling: I love it, but you might hate it. In any case, I doubt anyone is ambivalent. When first confronted with the Juke, my 3-year-old son remarked, “That car have lots of lights and eyes on it.” That’s as accurate a description of the Juke front end as you’ll get.
The face is dominated by bug-eye headlamps, and the running lights bulge up above the hood such that they’re in the driver’s line of sight. At night, the effect is of large bioluminescent slugs lounging atop the front fenders. Admittedly, it’s more appealing than I’m making it sound.
A front-drive, manual-shift Juke Nismo like my test car costs $2,000 more than the midlevel SV model, and that money nets comprehensive upgrades. The Nismo gets dark-finish 18-inch wheels (an inch larger than the standard Juke’s), new seats with more pronounced bolsters, stiffer suspension and a special front fascia and lower body cladding. If the Nismo’s 197 horsepower — nine more than the standard models — isn’t enough, the Juke Nismo RS, arriving in showrooms next month, will serve up 215 horses.
The Nismo’s steering wheel is wrapped in Alcantara — a nice fake suede — at the 3- and 9-o’clock positions, while the top and bottom sections are leather-clad. A red stripe denotes top dead center position. It wouldn’t look out of place in an $80,000 Porsche.
The gearshift, too, seems to hail from a different price class. The mechanism isn’t entirely frictionless, but its subtle feedback lets you know you’ve actually engaged a gear, not plunged a spoon into a bowl of gumbo. Each shift returns a satisfying little crunch of vibration through the shift knob, like stepping on a single Cheerio.
The Juke’s tachometer face is a dull iridescent red, while the speedometer is white-on-black. You know who else uses tachometers in that hue? A certain Italian company whose cars are often painted red. I’m guessing the similarity is not coincidental.
With the Designer Impostors tach, the racecar-style steering wheel and big bolsters on the Nismo-emblazoned seats, the mood is set for purposeful driving. And the Nismo delivers, with sharp steering and a suspension setup that prioritizes cornering over compliance. The 1.6-liter 4-cylinder delivers peak torque by 2,000 r.p.m., so the Juke feels strong even if you don’t wind it out to redline. It’s kind of fun, actually, to labor the motor at low r.p.m. and listen to the turbocharger huff and whoosh until you enter the power zone.
When the turbo’s full boost arrives, you might spin the front tires and incite axle hop, the spinning tires hammering up and down on the pavement until they regain traction. The solution to that problem would seem to be the all-wheel-drive option.
But you don’t want all-wheel-drive, because it’s available only with an automatic transmission. And the Juke automatic is a C.V.T. A performance car with a continuously variable transmission is like a bowl of your favorite spicy drunken noodles served with a bottle of ketchup. Please, I beseech you, go with the stick.
Last year Nissan enjoyed record sales, largely on the strength of its nonweird offerings. I hope that in the face of its mass-appeal success, Nissan keeps taking chances with endearing little oddballs like the Juke Nismo. Zog needs cars, too.
EZRA DYER

It goes back long before Wednesday night, when the 22-year-old
St. Louis Cardinals
pitcher Marco Gonzales was charged with three runs and the loss
in Game 4
of the National League Championship Series against the San Francisco Giants.
It goes back long before his stirring postseason run, when he won two games in the division series against the Los Angeles Dodgers and did not allow a run in his first five appearances.
For some of us, it goes back to junior high, with his mother, long before Gonzales was born.
“I’m sure he’s bummed they lost,” his mother, Gina, wrote in an email late Wednesday night. “But there’s a game tomorrow. I’m sure he’ll say that’s what they have to focus on!”
When Gonzales made his major league debut in June,
Section 136 at Coors Field in Denver
was filled with friends and relatives. There were supporters from Fort Collins, about an hour’s drive to the north, where Gonzales was born and reared. There were coaches and teammates from Gonzaga University, where Gonzales starred for three seasons. There was his father, Frank, a former professional pitcher and now a minor league coach.
And there was a woman holding a sign, made in jest by a family member, that read, “I’m just the mom.”
It was Gina, the only member of the family I know. She was a friend from junior high and high school. These days, our lives intersect only through the happenstance of Facebook posts, as so many old friendships do. In June, I was among those who congratulated her on her son’s success, and well wishes poured in from others. Soon, Marco Gonzales was demoted to the minors.
But in the final month of the season, he reappeared as a key player for St. Louis. In two starts and five relief appearances, beginning Aug. 30, he won four games down the stretch, and he won twice more in relief in an N.L. division series.
Then he showed up on my television over the weekend, standing on the mound in a taut game against the Giants, pitching another in a string of scoreless innings.

On Wednesday, the duties of a sports reporter melding with the curiosity of a friend, I called Gina. It was shortly before Game 4. Like light from a star, her voice and laugh might as well have been sent from years before. It sounded the same.
“It’s totally surreal,” she said of the past few weeks. “Totally bizarre.”
Then it got really weird. With the
Cardinals
holding a 4-3 lead, Gonzales entered in the sixth inning. He walked Juan Perez, then allowed a single to Brandon Crawford. A sacrifice bunt moved the runners to second and third.
Gregor Blanco grounded meekly to first baseman Matt Adams, whose off-balance throw home bounced, too late to catch Perez. The score was tied. Then Joe Panik grounded sharply to Adams, who stepped on first base and threw off-target to second. Crawford sprinted home with what held up as the winning run. San Francisco took a three-games-to-one lead in the series.

Who is this young pitcher, this Mario Lopez look-alike who improbably finds himself in the middle of the action?
On the phone, there was some catching up to do. After high school, Gina went to Colorado State. It was there that she met Frank Gonzales, a left-handed pitcher on the college team who became a 16th-round draft choice of the Detroit Tigers in 1989. He and Gina married in February 1990 and embarked on a nomadic life in baseball: 30 moves, seven states and five foreign countries (mostly for winter ball) before they bought their first house. Through most of it, they toted a son, Marco, born in 1992.
“We once added it up,” Gina said. “By the time Marco was in kindergarten, he had seen between 700 and 800 games. That’s what professional baseball people do.”
On occasion, the parents grabbed a night out. One of Marco’s first babysitters was a Fall League teammate of Frank’s in Arizona.
“I like to remind Marco that Mike Piazza used to change his diaper,” Gina said.
Frank Gonzales spent
10 years playing professional baseball
, including five seasons with Class AAA Toledo, one step from the majors. He never got the call to the major leagues. A lot of his battery mates did, though.
“He says that he made the catchers look good,” Gina said.
The family settled back to Fort Collins. Alex was born, six years behind Marco. At 16, he is now a promising player — catcher and infielder, mostly — at Rocky Mountain High School. When Marco was there, he was the winning pitcher in four straight state championship games.
Frank is a pitching coach for the Colorado Rockies’ Class A club. Gina is a firefighter, recently promoted to engineer, which means her duties now include driving.
A year before Gonzales was drafted by St. Louis, Alex bought him a Cardinals hat. At spring training this season, Alex predicted that Marco would pitch at Coors Field and strike out Troy Tulowitzki, which he did on three pitches in the first inning of his debut.
“Alex is kind of our prophet,” Gina said.
The Rockies had drafted Gonzales in high school, in the 29th round in 2010, but he opted to attend Gonzaga instead of signing. The Cardinals chose him last year with the 19th choice over all in the first round.
He was headed to the Class AA All-Star Game when the Cardinals ordered him to meet them in Colorado, to replace the injured pitcher Jaime Garcia. Gonzales called his mother, who had spent 10 years watching her husband try to get to the majors.
“I didn’t believe him,” Gina said. “I live in a house full of boys. There’s never a day that they don’t try to pull one over on me. He said, ‘I’m pitching at Coors Field on Wednesday.’ And I said, ‘No, you’re not.’ ”
Gonzales started three times, always reaching the fifth inning but absorbing two losses. He was sent to Class AAA Memphis, where he was 4-1 in July and August. St. Louis brought him back. On the strength of his fastball, changeup and fast-improving cutter, he was 4-0 in late September and earned a spot on the postseason roster.

His family is thrilled by his success but seems unaffected by the pressure. Frank was at the game in San Francisco. Gina, after traveling with the Cardinals the past couple of weeks, was back in Fort Collins with Alex. She watched Game 4 with friends at a bar.
“I look at him and go, ‘Well, there he is on the mound again,’ ” Gina said. “I’ve been watching him on the mound since he was 5 years old. To me, it’s just another day at the park. What’s surreal is everything else. Now there’s 50,000 people at the park.”
Gonzales was the Game 1 winner in the division series against the Dodgers, after the Los Angeles ace Clayton Kershaw was unexpectedly chased in a 10-9 St. Louis victory. Gonzales pitched a perfect seventh inning in Game 2. In Game 4, he pitched a scoreless top of the seventh inning; Matt Adams slugged a three-run homer in the bottom half to give the Cardinals the lead and Gonzales the victory.
Strong, scoreless performances continued in Games 1 and 3 against the Giants, though the Cardinals lost both games. When starters start to struggle, Manager Mike Matheny looks toward Gonzales.
Invariably, Gina’s phone buzzes as he reaches the mound. Friends want to tell her that her son is pitching.
“Yeah, I kind of know,” she said with a laugh. She is, after all, his mom.

Lynn R. Williams became head of the United Steel Workers union in 1983, early in one of the worst decades in history for steel and steelworkers in America.
Having lost much of its core business to better-equipped foreign competitors in the 1970s, the American steel industry had closed hundreds of mills since the new decade began, eliminating 200,000 jobs in the United States and Canada by 1983. It would eliminate 200,000 more by the decade’s end.
The bookish, Canadian-born Mr. Williams, who died May 5 in Toronto at 89, assumed control of a union that at 600,000 members was half the size it had been in 1979. In the next few years, he would steer members through round after round of layoffs, company bankruptcies and a six-month work stoppage at
U.S. Steel
. Yet by the time he retired in 1994, he also added 100,000 new members to the union’s ranks and pioneered strategies for carving lasting benefits for workers from the fast-shrinking industrial core of the American economy.
Mr. Williams was early to recognize the permanent nature of job losses in the steel industry, and one of the first to adopt a strategy of diversification. As U.S. Steel began buying oil companies, for instance, he led organizing campaigns that brought rubber, cork and linoleum workers, upholsterers, security guards, bus drivers and Canadian ski-patrol members into the ranks of the steelworkers.
His union was also among the first to successfully demand financial transparency from the industry to negotiate deals fair to both sides and the first to hire an investment bank (Lazard Frères) to provide advice on subjects like stock options, profit-sharing and how to leverage union power in takeover raids like Carl Icahn’s stormy 1986 bid for U.S. Steel.
In exchange for concessions on wages and benefits, Mr. Williams negotiated contract provisions that added union members to employee stock-ownership plans and gave them seats on the company board. He mediated bailouts that saved 25 steel plants from closing between 1985 and 1993 by leveraging employee stock holdings.
Mr. Williams, whose death was confirmed by the steelworkers union, was the first Canadian to head a major American industrial union.
He had been the union’s second-in-command for several years before being named president; and was already enmeshed in the union’s state-of-emergency efforts: He had negotiated wage and benefit concessions in hopes of saving jobs. He had coordinated food and clothing aid for unemployed members in towns where the mills had closed and supermarkets and stores of all kinds were leaving as well, for lack of business.
He had been working the phones for months, entreating friendly members of Congress to block a bill that would permit steel companies to void their labor contracts if they filed for bankruptcy. (The bill, long advocated by the steel industry, passed in 1984.)
For all his preparation, though, he said years later, Mr. Williams remembered feeling overwhelmed when, after the death of his predecessor, Lloyd McBride, of a heart attack, he suddenly became president of an enterprise under siege on so many fronts.
“If you can imagine an old mattress out in the junkyard with the springs popping up, I was like a guy lying on the springs trying to hold them all down,” Mr. Williams said in a 2010 interview, describing his first days in the job.
With only two hands, two legs and a torso, he added, “I didn’t have enough body parts.”

His interviews after retirement were often colorful. But his public statements during 11 years as union president bore the negotiator’s stamp of calculated dullness, said Harry C. Katz, dean of the School of Industrial and Labor Relations at Cornell University.
“He didn’t do quotes” for the newspapers, which made him less familiar to the public than some labor leaders of the time, Dr. Katz said. But he was known for a nuanced understanding of the economics of steelmaking, as well as his grasp of the wage earner’s world.
“He was ahead of the curve in so many ways,” Dr. Katz added. “He was probably one of the most intelligent labor leaders of the 20th century.”

Lynn Russell Williams was born into a devoutly religious family in rural Springfield, Ontario, on July 21, 1924, one of three children of the Rev. His father was a minister in the United Church of Canada, and his mother an ardent churchgoer who named her son after Lynn Harold Hough, a famous Methodist theologian of the early 20th century.
He originally planned to follow his father into the ministry. But after the church transferred his father to the industrial city of Hamilton during the Depression, Lynn was drawn to the growing union movement as a more “democratic” way of helping people.

After a year in the Royal Canadian Navy, he began his master’s degree in industrial relations and economics at the University of Toronto, but dropped out to take a job at a steel plant, and to join the union.

During the night of June 30, 1934, a unit of Heinrich Himmler’s Schutzstaffel (the SS), with logistical support from the German Army, pulled up outside a hotel in Bad Wiessee, south of Munich, and in Hitler’s presence hauled a bewildered Ernst Röhm, leader of the Nazi brownshirts (or SA), out of bed. He and his cronies were taken to Munich’s Stadelheim prison, where they were shot on the spot — except for Röhm, whose execution occurred shortly thereafter. Similar raids took place that night against other SA leaders, who were charged, like Röhm, with having planned a coup against Hitler and his government. In reality, this “Night of the Long Knives” was the violent end to power struggles between Hitler and the army officer corps on the one hand, and Röhm, as the head of roughly two million paramilitary storm troopers, on the other. They had challenged Hitler’s absolute leadership and also the professional officer corps’s claim to be the sole bearer of arms in Nazi Germany.
All in all, about 85 people were killed over the next three days. Among them was Dr. Karl-Günther Heimsoth, one of Röhm’s lovers. His death revealed another facet of Nazi brutality, a vicious homophobia. Under the Reich, homosexual men were subjected to persecution, deemed decadent misfits who could be “cured” only by harsh “education.” Homosexuals thus became yet another minority that was discriminated against, incarcerated and killed. An estimated 100,000 were arrested, and as many as 15,000 were eventually sent to concentration camps, where they were identified by a pink triangle sewn on their prison uniforms. Thousands of them perished.
Robert Beachy’s excellent and richly documented new book, “Gay Berlin: Birthplace of a Modern Identity,” merely touches on these horrors. Instead, he takes the reader to the other end of the spectrum of opinion — that homosexuality is and has always been a sexual orientation fixed from birth, that same-sex love is as normal as heterosexuality, a condition not amenable to treatment but rather an endowment of nature that should be respected as part of a person’s identity.
No less important, Beachy, a professor of history at Goucher College in Baltimore, locates the origins of this view of human sexuality in Germany in the mid-19th century, in a culture that also produced modern scientific sexological research. His book carefully evaluates the arguments of a number of individuals in this period who wrote about the subject and agitated for the abolition of the widespread legal discriminations of the time.
As elsewhere in Europe, the enforcement of anti-gay laws was an issue, and here the book contains a surprise. While other German cities pursued stricter policies, it was in Prussian Berlin, under a police commissioner named Leopold von Meerscheidt-Hüllessem, that more liberal policies were adopted, a development that occurred after undercover officers concluded that private clubs and bars for homosexuals were peaceful establishments and did not constitute a public threat or nuisance. Only male prostitution (often related to female prostitution, organized crime and blackmail) was vigorously prosecuted. Consequently, pre-1914 Berlin developed a flourishing subculture in which homosexuals congregated without fear of arrest. Hüllessem also promoted cooperation with Dr. Magnus Hirschfeld, an internationally renowned pioneer in sexological research, who became a driving force behind a lobby for legal reform.

The German-born American physician Harry Benjamin, who met Hirschfeld in 1907, frequently returned to Berlin and later wrote on transsexuality in the United States. Another supporter, who became a member of Hirschfeld’s Scientific Humanitarian Committee, was Willibald Baron von Sattler-Grün, known as “the Baroness,” who usually turned up for the group’s meetings in drag. Soon the Social Democratic Party and the liberal press supported a program advanced by Hirschfeld’s organization, aimed at convincing a broader public that same-sex love was a legitimate expression of human sexuality and personhood. Activists organized popular assemblies, often in working-class districts, that attracted up to a thousand curious listeners, evidently keen to learn more.
Beachy’s study contains a fascinating chapter on pre-1914 “outing” scandals, the most notorious of which ultimately led to the conviction of one of the emperor’s closest friends, Philipp Prince zu Eulenburg-Hertefeld, though not for illicit homosexuality. Rather, Eulenburg was found to have perjured himself during an acrimonious libel suit when he denied his homosexuality. Another interesting chapter, which focuses on the homoerotic and homosexual bonding of adolescents in the Wandervogel youth movement, includes an analysis of the writings of Hans Blüher, one of its leaders. For Blüher, male friendship, not heterosexual partnership, was the true foundation of human society.
The years after World War I brought increased activism and were a busy time for Hirschfeld and his associates. Supported by Helene Stöcker, a leading feminist, and the Social Democrats, his large institute and many followers started a massive research project, studying the many varieties of sexual identity, including lesbian, bisexual and transgender behaviors and outlooks. Journals, magazines and films on these topics proliferated in the liberal urban climate of Weimar Germany. During this time, Hirschfeld’s colleague Richard Linsert undertook a detailed survey of male prostitution, based on several hundred interviews. Some gender reassignment operations were also attempted, but had to be abandoned as too risky and controversial.
The significance of Beachy’s book goes beyond his findings on the German roots of the conclusion that homosexuality is a biologically fixed trait. Beachy’s work must also be considered in the larger context of a shift in cultural studies. Both the Wilhelmine and Weimar periods are no longer seen — as they were in the early post-1945 decades — as an autocratic divergence from the Western liberal-­democratic model of political and sociocultural development that culminated in Nazism. Notwithstanding many elements of a traditional authoritarianism, Weimar was a modern society, one that France, Britain and the United States could in some ways be seen as lagging behind. Rather than viewing the 1920s as a period that led inevitably to the Nazi dictatorship, many historians now study the contradictions of Weimar modernity, with Berlin seen as a major center of political, socioeconomic and cultural diversity.
To be sure, the balance between Hirschfeld’s findings and their rejection by his opponents remained precarious, and in 1933, with Hitler’s rise to power, it tipped over into a regime that murdered millions of innocent human beings. Given the extremism of the Nazi solution to human difference, it took the Germans quite a long time after 1945 to reach the sort of openness and tolerance that had existed in “Gay Berlin” before 1914.

BRIDGEWATER, Conn. —  Forget last week’s small-potato questions of who should govern or represent the people of Connecticut.
Here, the big news on Tuesday was that this tradition-bound town of 1,725, which prides itself on an annual tractor parade down Main Street and the handmade chocolates that bear its name in shapes like Pilgrims’ hats, was at long last prepared to relinquish the bragging rights of being the last dry town in Connecticut since the adoption of Prohibition almost a century ago.
With 73 percent of those registered participating, Bridgewater’s voters overwhelmingly agreed to strike down the town’s long-held ban on the sale of alcohol, 660 to 246.
Change will not come immediately, however. For starters, the town’s zoning laws do not currently allow restaurants or cafes inside its borders.
Still, residents saw the vote as long overdue.
“Bridgewater was an anomaly,” Curtis S. Read, the town’s first selectman, said on Thursday from Town Hall. He snagged the top job last year by promising residents that he would work to bring a “little bit of progress,” as he put it, to their sleepy town, just northeast of Danbury.
Others, however, prefer the town the way the way it is: the kind of dreamy place where everyone pitches in on the annual fair that supports the volunteer firehouse and shows up in force for the tractor parade.
Steve Shabet, a farmer whose float once won a prize in the parade (it tossed green beans to spectators along the route), said he was drawn to Bridgewater from the Upper West Side by “the quietness of the farms and the friendliness of its people.” Nonetheless, he supported the ballot measure as a way “to attract more young families.” Not eager to see the town’s one elementary school be consolidated into a regional one, he said, “You need more infrastructure and services, and one would be a nice restaurant for casual dining.”
The lack of commercial activity in Bridgewater, beyond a few establishments such as a gas station and a village store that sells baked goods and other treats, means that the sale of alcohol is still theoretical.
The ballot measure envisions nothing more than eventually allowing “the sale of alcoholic liquor in all establishments operating under restaurant or cafe permits” during specified hours. The town’s zoning will have to be reassessed before there is a restaurant for anyone to run up a tab.
The measure in no way allows the sale of alcohol in convenience stores or the establishment of liquor stores.
Mr. Read, who has an undergraduate degree in French literature and a master’s in agriculture, is as fond as the next flannel-shirted farmer of the old ways of doing things. He has worked as a shepherd, rancher and conservationist and came to Connecticut in 1981 to help the state promote sheep farming.
But he is among those who felt that if the town stayed dry, it would also watch its future dry up. Enrollment in the town’s elementary school through grade five, now 75 children, has been dipping, threatening the school’s viability, and
the average age
of the town’s residents is in the 50s, about a dozen years higher than in Connecticut as a whole. With so few people around, staffing the firehouse and other local organizations can be a challenge, one reason many civic-minded residents wear multiple hats.

As the man who doubles as police chief, Mr. Read said he was not especially moved by opponents’ arguments, made at town meetings, that the community would see a spike in drunken driving or rowdiness.
Drinking inside one’s home or at local gatherings is legal, and even the local volunteer firefighters hosted a “wine and beer tasting” event on a recent Saturday.
Some residents expressed unease that the change was being pushed through, less for the benefit of most locals than for the benefit of some of the town’s wealthier residents who might profit from it, and for New Yorkers who descend upon the town on weekends. “Just because we now have liquor sales isn’t what I call revitalization of a town,” said William T. Stuart, Mr. Read’s predecessor as first selectman and originator of the tractor parade. “It will take a lot more to revitalize it.”
One target of the opponent’s ire has been Peter W. May, a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist who sits on many of New York’s most prestigious boards, including Mount Sinai Health System and Carnegie Hall. He is one of two businessmen with ties to the community who have expressed eagerness to open a restaurant that would serve alcohol, if allowed.
Mr. May, 71, and his wife, Leni, stumbled upon Bridgewater 38 years ago and have extended their 11-acre country home until they had 1,100 acres.
Known as Maywood, the property is filled with gardens; apple orchards; beehives; and a vineyard that has been producing 1,500 bottles a year of chardonnay and cabernet franc.
Town officials say the Mays are their biggest taxpayers, and they are grateful to the couple for stepping up roughly 25 years ago to buy the town’s sole village store when it was on the ropes. It is the one place where locals can pick up homemade bread, treats and produce, grown on Mr. May’s farm. On school days, the tin-roofed store stays open until the last schoolchild is picked up.
“He’s our main benefactor,” Mr. Read said of Mr. May.
According to Mr. May, who did not get to vote on Tuesday because he is registered in New York, the store has racked up close to $1.5 million in losses. “I sort of think of that as my contribution to the town,” he said.
He understands that some critics have been saying that he backed the proposal so he could make a fortune on the property, an assertion he finds laughable. “Whatever attitude they might have about me,” he said, “this is a bigger issue. It’s about trying to make the town more vibrant.”

About 30 minutes before the start of Karl Ove Knausgaard’s event at the relatively small and narrow Community Bookstore in Park Slope on Wednesday, people packed the entire space in a scene more reminiscent of the calm before an indie-rock storm than an author appearance. Ezra Goldstein, an owner of the store, approached a microphone. “Don’t get excited,” he said. “This is just a sound check.”
Mr. Knausgaard, the Norwegian writer whose Proustian six-volume autobiographical novel, “My Struggle,” has become an unlikely hit (the third volume translated in English was
released last week in the United States
) is in New York for events with three high-profile peers. His first stop, a conversation with the novelist Nicole Krauss, was in Park Slope on Wednesday night. He will speak to Zadie Smith at McNally Jackson bookstore in SoHo on Thursday night, and to Jeffrey Eugenides at the New York Public Library on Friday.
When he started writing “My Struggle,”  Mr. Knausgaard said during the interview on Wednesday, “I didn’t really know what my life was like.” He called the book “a search,” and said, “I didn’t find anything.”
Ms. Krauss said she read the first book in the series without expectations, and was “absolutely stunned” by its candor and pacing, which both felt “reckless.”
“In order to be free, I needed to write very quickly and get rid of the notion of quality,” Mr. Knausgaard said. At first he was writing five pages a day, then 10 and eventually 20.
He chalked up the interest in the quotidian concerns of “My Struggle” to the transformative power of literature. “If I told you my life story here and now, in this bookstore, you might leave me after 10 or 15 minutes,” he told Ms. Krauss. “It would be unbearable.”
Ms. Krauss said she was “sick of plot and characters and dialogue and scenes and climax and resolution” in traditional novels, and that Mr. Knausgaard had “reinvented and surpassed the form of the novel” through “radical attentiveness.” Mr. Knausgaard said he shared her fatigue with more conventional stories. “Form is, in a way, death,” he said. “A novelist’s obligation is to break free from the form, even though he knows that this will also be seen as artificial and distanced from life.”
Michael Nagle for The New York Times
Mr. Knausgaard during his conversation with the novelist Nicole Krauss on Wednesday night.
Answering a question about the hazards of writing about real people, he looked genuinely pained, and said reactions from family and other people depicted in the books had ranged from “very, very generous to very, very angry.” (In
a recent interview
in The New Republic, he said, “The difficult thing for me is that I want basically to be a good man. That’s what I want to be. In this project, I wasn’t. It is unmoral, in a way.”) “I’m giving away my family’s story,” he said on Wednesday night. “Who owns the family’s story? I don’t. But you could turn it around and ask, ‘Who is to deny me to write my family’s story?’ I have hurt people, but I don’t think in a dangerous way. But you can’t tell.”
After the reading, Mr. Knausgaard smoked a cigarette on the outdoor patio behind the store. He said he had no explanation for his project’s success in America, which he called “amazing.” “When I talk to people about these books,” he said, “they’ll say one sentence about the book and then something about their lives, about their alcoholic father or something.” That connection with readers is “what you’re looking for, no matter what kind of author you are.”
Mr. Knausgaard has developed a sizable following, but there are plenty more readers to win over. For the final question of the night from an audience member, Ms. Krauss pointed to a man who appeared to be in his 50s wearing a baseball cap pulled low over his eyes. “I came here without knowing about you,” he said to Mr. Knausgaard. “What’s your book about? What would you want people to know about you and your life?” Mr. Knausgaard paused and the audience laughed, thinking about the informative interview that had just wrapped up and of the 3,600 soul-searching pages for which the man was seeking summary.
“This is a normal book about a normal life,” Mr. Knausgaard finally responded. “That’s not a great sales pitch, but it’s the best I have.”

“Serial,”
the blockbuster investigative podcast, ended its first season two weeks ago after gripping millions of listeners this fall with a 15-year-old murder mystery in Maryland.
But the story of “Serial” got an unexpected twist this week when the website
The Intercept published an interview with Jay Wilds
, a central figure in the case who had declined to be interviewed on the record by Sarah Koenig, the creator of “Serial.”
In the original case, Adnan Syed, a high school student, was convicted of killing Hae Min Lee, his 18-year-old former girlfriend, in early 1999. Mr. Wilds, a friend, had been a key witness at the trial, saying that Mr. Syed had told him about the killing and that he had helped Mr. Syed bury Ms. Lee’s body in a Baltimore park.
On Monday afternoon, The Intercept — an investigative website that is part of First Look Media, founded last year with a $250 million investment by Pierre Omidyar, the billionaire founder of eBay — posted a 3,400-word transcript of what it said was the first of a “multipart interview” with Mr. Wilds. In that first segment, Mr. Wilds repeated assertions he had made at trial that Mr. Syed told him he killed Ms. Lee, and also recounted the story of the two men burying her body.
Mr. Wilds attributed any inconsistencies in his story to his initial unwillingness to cooperate with the police. As a low-level drug dealer, he said, he was convinced that “the cops are going to fry me.”
He also referred to the historical mistrust of the police among blacks in Baltimore. “This is where the ‘Stop Snitching’ video comes from,” Mr. Wilds said. “This is where people would have their house firebombed and still tell the police they knew nothing about it rather than to try to make some sense of what’s going on. And that’s not necessarily me — but that is my family, that is my uncles and cousins. It’s where I’m from.”
After getting wide attention online for Part 1 of the interview, The Intercept said on Tuesday that it was preparing to post Part 2, and teased that the new segment would explain Mr. Wilds’s refusal to speak to “Serial.”
“Serial,” which began in October and continued for 12 weekly episodes, became the fastest podcast to reach five million downloads, according to Apple, and the show is estimated to have generated 40 million downloads over all. The show was a spinoff of “This American Life,” the public radio show on which Ms. Koenig has been a longtime producer.
Natasha Vargas-Cooper, who conducted the interview, answered a few questions on
Twitter
on Monday about how she secured the scoop and how The Intercept interacted with Mr. Wilds. “A fellow journalist put me in touch with Jay,” she wrote. “I wanted to hear his side and he asked me a lot of questions and I asked him questions.”
“Jay was not paid to do the interview,” Ms. Vargas-Cooper added. “We do not pay our sources.”

For Alex Pincus, the question wasn’t whether Manhattan needed a floating oyster bar and mini-maritime museum on a 72-year-old codfish schooner, but rather where to put it. Now, his vision has become reality in the form of
Grand Banks
, which will begin serving food and drinks Thursday afternoon on a boat docked off Hudson River Park in TriBeCa.
Pincus, who grew up sailing on Lake Pontchartrain and founded the
Atlantic Yachting
school on the Upper West Side with his brother Miles, had been reading about the city’s 19th-century oyster barges a few years ago when the idea occurred to him to build a modern-day version. Piled high with just-dug Crassostrea virginica, says Pincus, the vessels would sell their wares to hungry New Yorkers directly from the docks. “We thought, ‘why don’t we have that here?’” he says of a conversation with Miles that followed. The two gathered their restaurant-industry friends — including Mark Firth, a co-founder of the Brooklyn restaurants
Diner
and
Marlow & Sons
and Adrien Gallo, a former owner of downtown bars including Palais Royale and Double Happiness — and “started looking around for the spot.”
That spot turned out to be the park’s Pier 25, where the partners have a yearlong lease to park a 142-foot-long Nova Scotian wooden fishing vessel called the Sherman Zwicker. (Tentative plans are to stay until fall, says Alex Pincus, and then sail down to Florida for the winter.)
The Sherman Zwicker was once the property of the
Maine Maritime Museum
, where four decades ago a sailor and nautical-history buff named George McEvoy (“the ultimate old soul,” says Pincus) lovingly restored it. As of last week McEvoy’s pride and joy — the last of its kind used to fish among the Grand Banks of Newfoundland and now the largest wooden vessel in New York City — was docked in Red Hook, Brooklyn. There the Pincuses and their partners hustled to outfit the kitchen (formerly bunks where sailors slept) and to prepare marine-education exhibits in the stalls where just-caught cod was once buried in salt for the trip to South America.
Above decks, they also built out two bars, one for drinks (such as daily nautical-themed cocktails and ales from Red Hook’s Other Half Brewing Company), and another topped with zinc for a rotating menu of sustainably sourced oysters. Those, as well as the rest of the Grand Banks menu — lobster rolls, small plates of seasonally and locally available seafood — will be overseen by Firth, who is also the owner of
Prairie Whale
restaurant in the Berkshires.
It was in those landlocked mountains, where both Firth and Alex Pincus had moved a few years back, that the seed for Grand Banks was first planted. The two men, old friends from the city, crossed paths at the gym and got to discussing how they shared both a love of the urban waterfront and a desire to connect the rest of the city to it. It was that conversation that spurred Pincus to research old New York’s oyster barges. Now, both are splitting their time between the boat and the Berkshires. “It’s kind of ironic that we had to move away,” says Firth, “to figure this out.”

One patient was found dead in his bed from an overdose, with a prescription for painkillers from a Queens doctor on the night stand. Another was discovered lifeless and slumped over in his car, a pill bottle naming the same doctor under his body.
The doctor,
Stan Xuhui Li
, 60, ran a weekend pain-management clinic from a basement office in Flushing, where he saw as many as 90 patients a day, so many he gave them numbers as if they were at a delicatessen, prosecutors said. He accepted only cash. A price list was posted on the wall: Three prescriptions for 120 pills cost $100.
Among Dr. Li’s patients, prosecutors say, were drug addicts and street dealers who knew they could get a prescription, with few questions asked, for the right price. One patient was
David S. Laffer
, an addict who in June 2011 massacred four people while stealing narcotics from a drugstore in Medford, N.Y., on Long Island. He is now serving life without parole. Dr. Li, through his lawyer, has previously denied selling drugs to Mr. Laffer.
On Wednesday, the opening day of Dr. Li’s trial in State Supreme Court in Manhattan, he was accused of giving prescriptions for opiates like OxyContin and tranquilizers like Xanax to people he knew were abusing drugs, ignoring warnings from their doctors and relatives that they might overdose.
The office of New York City’s special narcotics prosecutor is handling the case. Under a novel theory rarely used in the state, Dr. Li has been charged with two counts of second-degree manslaughter and seven counts of reckless endangerment, as well as 180 counts of illegally selling prescriptions for narcotics. The top charges carry a maximum possible penalty of 15 years in prison.
The 218-count indictment concerns Dr. Li’s treatment of 20 patients from 2004 to 2011; at least four of them died. The doctor is also accused of defrauding
Medicare
and an insurance company, billing for exams he never performed, and of falsifying documents given to regulators.
“This is a case about a doctor who put money before lives, and not just any lives — lives with which he was entrusted,” an assistant district attorney, Charlotte Fishman, told the jury.
Dr. Li’s lawyer, Raymond Belair, said that his client had been deceived by some patients, but that Dr. Li had acted in good faith, prescribing the proper dosages for their complaints. The people who died failed to follow instructions, Mr. Belair said.
“No one who took the medications that Dr. Li prescribed as he prescribed them got into any trouble in this case,” Mr. Belair said. “Patients didn’t follow instructions and went to do things that Dr. Li had no way of knowing about.”
Mr. Belair said Dr. Li’s records would show that he regularly tried to wean patients off painkillers or reduce their dependence. He stopped seeing some patients who broke a promise to cut back on painkillers, the lawyer said.
“There is a persistent pattern here that speaks to good faith,” he said.
Dr. Li was born in China and attended medical school there. In the United States, he received board certification in anesthesiology and pain management. Before his arrest in November 2011, he was a staff anesthesiologist at Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital in New Jersey.
But one day each weekend, Ms. Fishman said, Dr. Li operated the clinic in Flushing, where he owned two condominiums. It was highly lucrative. Each week Dr. Li made cash deposits of $1,000 to $14,000 at three banks in New Jersey, Ms. Fishman said. His cash deposits totaled $450,000 in one two-year period, she said.

Phil Klay won the National Book Award for fiction on Wednesday night for his debut short story collection, “Redeployment,” which draws on his experience serving as a Marine in Iraq and captures the terror, boredom and occasionally the humorous side of war.
In an emotional acceptance speech, Mr. Klay described returning from the war and being treated as if he were unstable, and being asked by children if he had killed anyone.
“I came back not knowing what to think,” he said. “What do you do when you’re trying to explain in words, to the father of a fallen Marine, exactly what that Marine meant to you?”
He said writing fiction about his experiences helped him to process it. “I can’t think of a more important conversation to be having,” he said. “War is too strange to be processed alone.”
Some of the stories, which were published by Penguin Press, take place in Anbar Province, while others are set in the United States as soldiers struggle to readjust to civilian life.
In the nonfiction category, Evan Osnos, a staff writer for The New Yorker, won for “Age of Ambition: Chasing Fortune, Truth and Faith in the New China,” published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux. The book explores China’s ongoing transformation into an economic superpower, and the clash between its economic progress and its authoritarian government’s crackdown on social freedoms.
In an acceptance speech, Mr. Osnos thanked his Chinese subjects for taking a risk by talking to him. “They live in a place where it’s very dangerous to be honest and be vulnerable,” he said.
The awards were presented at a black-tie dinner at Cipriani Wall Street, with more than 700 guests attending a ceremony hosted by Daniel Handler, better known as the children’s book author Lemony Snicket.

The National Book Award, which was established in 1950, is one of the country’s most prestigious and coveted literary prizes. Books written by American authors and published between Dec. 1, 2013, and Nov. 30, 2014, were eligible this year.
Jacqueline Woodson, a three-time finalist, won the young people’s literature award for her memoir in verse, “Brown Girl Dreaming,” which detailed her experience growing up as an African-American in South Carolina and New York during the 1960s and ’70s. To capture the spirit of the “reformicons” for the July 6
cover story about the emerging band of intellectuals in the Republican Party
, Eric Ogden photographed members of the group in Gunston Hall, the historic mansion in Virginia that belonged to George Mason. Ogden’s group portrait, which alluded to paintings of the founding fathers, inspired readers to analyze who was included (“This is the Republican idea of diversity?”) and what they were doing (“Who’s going to sweep up that mess on the floor? The rest of the country?”). Ogden recently discussed how the photo came about — and what’s on those pages on the floor.
What inspired you to pose the subjects in this way?
I was trying to create an interesting composition and have them interrelate. In a way, “The Last Supper” was popping into my head. When I told them this, I told them that they shouldn’t read into it, that it’s just a visual reference. There are often biblical paintings where there’s the main characters, and off in the periphery there’s the supporting cast, and they’re often having their own aside. If this was a Shakespearean play, they would be having conversations, whispering or looking off into the corner of a room as someone walks in. There’s a lot to look at, and it tells a story.
Were any of the poses improvised?
I asked them if they had any personal props that I thought could be interesting. James Pethokoukis was the first person to say, “I have my iPad.” I gave everyone, individually, their own direction, which is what I sometimes do when photographing large groups. And then I’ll step back and call action. The tall woman, Kate O’Beirne, said, “I’d like to be looking over somebody’s shoulder, or can I put my hand on his shoulder and look over there?” I thought that was great. I like it when people get into it.
Inquiring minds want to know what the papers on the floor contain.

.”
Was it a reference to Jean Leon Gerome Ferris’s painting “

Women are big this election season. No group is more courted. It’s great! The issues are important. Plus, we all enjoy the occasional pander.
Candidates are re-interpreting their old arguments in a new, woman-centric way. In Michigan, the Democratic Senate candidate defines his opponent’s opposition to Obamacare as a plan to “cut women’s access to ... mammograms.” In Kentucky, Republican Mitch McConnell has female surrogates claiming that his opponent, Alison Grimes, is trying to convince women that they “can’t graduate from college without raising your taxes.” This appears to be an oblique reference to Grimes’s call for reduced rates on student loans.
The College Republican National Committee has been investing heavily in online ads aimed at fans of the TV show “Say Yes to the Dress,” in which the dresses are named after gubernatorial candidates. If you are in, say, Florida, you’ll see a happy young woman trying on wedding gowns, twirling around and announcing that “The Rick Scott is perfect,” while her irritating mother demands that she take the Charlie Crist dress, even though it’s unflattering and costs more money. As a writer in Jezebel noted, it seems to have been made by people who felt the best way to communicate with female voters is “to explain things in terms of bridal wear.”
In Colorado, some commentators have given Democrat Mark Udall the nickname “Mark Uterus” because Udall has run so hard on women’s reproductive rights. It is definitely true that Udall has devoted a prodigious amount of ad-time to the fact that his opponent, Representative Cory Gardner, is a longtime supporter of the personhood movement, which declares all fertilized eggs are human beings. Voters find this idea so unnerving that a personhood amendment to the Constitution was soundly defeated in
Mississippi
. As well as Colorado, twice. Where it is on the ballot in November, yet again.
Gardner said he had changed his mind about the state constitutional amendment after it was overwhelmingly rejected in 2010 and he suddenly realized that it would have an effect on contraceptives. KATONAH, N.Y. — The most famous aria of Donizetti’s “Lucrezia Borgia” is the title character’s last. In “Era desso il figlio mio,” the power-hungry femme fatale of the title laments the loss of her son, whom she has unwittingly poisoned, in an explosion of vocal fireworks. It’s also an aria that Donizetti cut when he revised the opera in 1840, seven years after its Milan premiere, in an attempt to focus the drama more sharply.
On Saturday evening, in the Bel Canto series of the Caramoor Festival, the soprano Angela Meade dispatched the dizzying difficulties of “Era desso il figlio mio” with aplomb at the end of a powerful concert performance of “Borgia.” She reprises the role on Friday, but this time with the opera’s 1840 ending — sans fireworks.
For the scholar-conductor Will Crutchfield, it’s the sort of have-your-cake-and-eat-it luxury that comes with his territory. The Bel Canto series, which he leads, has both first-rate soloists familiar from major opera houses and a try-it-out spirit that is normally the preserve of academic and boutique productions. By pairing Donizetti’s “Borgia” with Verdi’s “Rigoletto” next weekend, Mr. Crutchfield explores the interconnectivity of these two Victor Hugo-inspired operas. In offering alternate endings of the Donizetti, he draws attention to the dramatic gravity of a composer often dismissed as a showman.
The preposterous but not incoherent plot centers on the relationship of Lucrezia and Gennaro, the son she concealed, who grew up knowing his mother only through her letters. His closest friend and ally is Maffio Orsini, leader of a group of hotheaded youngsters who nurse a burning hatred for the Borgias and who end up drawing her murderous wrath not only on themselves but also on Gennaro.
By force of personality, Lucrezia dominates every scene of the opera — even the ones without her. With her extraordinarily powerful and multifaceted soprano, Ms. Meade managed to do the same vocally, standing out from the excellent cast and focusing the energy of each ensemble on her. In the beginning, her high notes had a sharp edge; but in the course of the evening, her singing gained noticeably in warmth and pliancy. Her intelligent command of both text and melodic architecture helped knit the coloratura passages into a coherent musical structure.
Orsini is a trouser role, here sung by the charismatic mezzo Tamara Mumford, who has an aristocratic middle range, dusky depths and great confidence as an actress. Her “Nella fatal di Rimini” is the first aria of the opera; dark, intense and suspenseful, it establishes a sense of dramatic urgency that runs through the work.
The tenor Michele Angelini brought lyricism and vigor to the part of Gennaro. Perhaps more than any other principal, he seemed to have internalized the Bel Canto style to such a degree that his utterances felt natural and discursive. Christophoros Stamboglis was a formidable Duke of Ferrara (Lucrezia’s husband), combining a powerful bass with a discerning ear for phrasing.
The minor parts were ably sung by members of the Bel Canto Young Artists program; the men’s choruses, important for the overall dark coloring of the opera, were excellent. Under Mr. Crutchfield’s direction, the Orchestra of St. Luke’s played well, with occasional coordination problems and imbalances forgotten by the last act.

Editor’s Note: The author is a Pashto woman in her early 20’s who lives in Peshawar. Her name is withheld for safety.
I have heard my elders call Peshawar the city of flowers. But since Dec. 16, this feels like the city of the walking dead; a city whose flower-like children were crushed brutally when the Taliban attacked a school. At least 145 students and faculty members were killed in horrific ways; my tongue shivers to describe the atrocities. The death toll may be in hundreds but the entire city — the entire nation — feels like it lost its own loved ones.
The morning after Dec. 16 revealed the sight of funeral prayers everywhere. The students that survived were interviewed so much that they now plead not to be asked more questions as they get nightmares.
Occasional blasts and killings had become a part of life in Peshawar, but this is nothing like anything we know. It has been a week, yet no one can recover or function properly. Some call it a Black Day, while others call it the 9/11 of Pakistan. Whatever it was, it shook Pakistan at its core.
It has frequently been pointed out on the Internet that this massacre occurred because “the students went to school.” But it must be clarified that this occurred as revenge by the Taliban for the Zarb-e-Azb military operation that is being carried by the Pakistan Army. Since this school primarily consisted of children from Army families, the Taliban made it a battleground against the unarmed innocents.
A teacher of mine who lost his nephew in this massacre, Hassan Mustafa, says, “Keep praying for all the precious souls we lost and for those who will carry this heartbreaking pain for long. But we need to do more now, as acting now or never is the only option left!”
Pakistan is known for its love of conspiracies, provincial disputes and every random reason it can possibly find to argue. There are very few occasions when I have seen my country come together. This Black Day was one such day that the whole country united to put an end to this filth. There is no talk of a good or a bad religion, because nothing can justify what happened! There is no Pashtun, no Punjabi, no Sindhi, no Balochi and no political affiliation. From the valleys of Khyber to the plains of Karachi, every house mourns and stands together.
The Taliban will surely pay. They miserably failed in avenging the army. In fact, the country fell in love with its soldiers. Many of the children survivors pledge to join the army and make the Taliban pay for what they did to their friends and teachers. General Raheel Sharif, the Pakistan Chief of Army Staff, stood as a hero for us in this time of crisis. The common man is not afraid of death anymore, but he dreams of one thing: eliminating all terrorists.
As an immediate impact, the political leadership came together and reinstated the death penalty. At least six major terrorist criminals have been hanged to death and a few more are to be hanged in the coming days. Some international organizations are raising concerned eyebrows over Pakistan carrying out death penalties, but the masses, including some prominent international figures, believe this is vital in the given situation. The attitude of our people also has changed. Before, many in Pakistan believed this was a foreign war being fought on our land. These are the repercussions of the Western wars fought in these lands. But now it’s equally our war, because it is our children who are dying and our lives that are at stake.
For the first time, people are talking openly against the Taliban in public. I, being outspoken, was always told by my father to use “sensible and safe” words when talking on matters related to the issue. But the country isn’t afraid now. After all, there is already no guarantee of life. Still, both the main parties of Pakistan are sensible and still not brave enough to mention the terrorists by the name.
There is a dire need for the political parties to stand on one front against the Taliban and their allies. In fact, the whole world needs to come together. Every nation must pledge and make sure that its grounds will not be used for planning terrorist activities against any other nation, because terrorism cannot be limited by boundaries. Pakistan, Afghanistan and the United States, in particular, need to come up with a joint strategy. They must understand that there is no good or bad terrorist. All are equally dangerous.
Pakistan may be going through a rough time, but the world should know we are a brave nation. If England, Sri Lanka and other countries can put an end to violence in their countries, so can Pakistan!

FRANKFURT — Inflation in the eurozone fell in July to its lowest level since 2009, according to an official estimate released Thursday. But separate figures showing a drop in unemployment provided some reassurance that the region was not yet on the brink of a destructive downward price spiral.
The annual inflation rate in the 18 countries of the eurozone was 0.4 percent in July, according to a
preliminary estimate by Eurostat
, the European Union statistics agency, down from 0.5 percent in June.
That was the lowest inflation rate since October 2009, and remained well below the 2 percent rate that the European Central Bank considers healthy for the eurozone economy.
Economists and policy makers have worried that the eurozone is perilously close to a broad decline in prices known as deflation, which could undercut corporate revenues and profits, and lead to higher joblessness.
Those concerns have been amplified by signs that
tensions between Russia and Ukraine
could hurt the European economy by undercutting trade and creating uncertainty that would prevent businesses from investing and consumers from spending.
Fears of deflation may be partly offset by the decline in unemployment to 11.5 percent in June, from 11.6 percent in May. Joblessness fell in all of the countries that had been hardest hit by the euro crisis, including Greece, Ireland, Italy, Portugal, and Spain.
Unemployment rose in France, however, to 10.2 percent, from 10.1 percent. The increase is likely to bolster concerns that France is stuck in an economic rut and politically incapable of making changes to labor rules or putting in place other overhauls needed to improve economic performance.
Spain and Greece continued to have the highest unemployment in the eurozone, however. The jobless rate in Spain was 24.5 percent in June; in Greece, it was 27.3 percent in April, the most recent figures available. The lowest unemployment rates for the month of June were in Austria, at 5 percent, and Germany, at 5.1 percent.
Economists say the eurozone unemployment rate is still too high to put pressure on employers to raise wages, which would also raise inflation.
“Today’s figures don’t give any assurance that the eurozone is already out of the deflation danger zone,” Peter Vanden Houte, an economist at ING Bank in Brussels, wrote in a note to clients. “Moreover, with the escalating conflict with Russia dampening growth prospects, it seems unlikely that deflation fears will disappear any time soon.”
The drop in overall prices, which was in line with analyst forecasts, was caused by a fall in the inflation rate for food and tobacco, Eurostat said, as well as in energy prices.
Prices of industrial goods excluding energy were unchanged, while service prices rose at a rate of 1.3 percent, perhaps reflecting higher wage increases in Germany.

All ballet companies have their self-contradictions.
Boston Ballet
is both a much better company than it allowed New York to see last week in its season at the David H. Koch Theater and, occasionally, a more dismaying one. The troupe has the world’s finest current production of “The Sleeping Beauty,” at least two of America’s best classical ballerinas (Kathleen Breen Combes and Misa Kuranaga, wholly unalike), a staging of Balanchine’s “Jewels” with (as seen in 2009) several exhilarating points of text and style absent from New York City Ballet’s, and many other productions that make me wish I had time to visit Boston more often. Its choice of ballets by living choreographers is, however, much more problematic.
The company opened its season last week at the Koch Theater with a triple bill of works in which it was hard to care who was dancing, since each ballet made its performers look insincere, horrid or foolish. With the four highly dissimilar ballets of program B, on Friday, things became far more complex.
In Balanchine’s high-energy, structurally elaborate “Symphony in Three Movements” (1972), the dancers had a worthy challenge. The ballet had its premiere in this very theater as part of City Ballet’s Stravinsky Festival and has been regularly danced there by that company ever since. Nijinsky’s “Afternoon of a Faun” (1912), extraordinarily concentrated in focus, is largely two-dimensional in physical style (the dancers perpetually move through bas-relief positions). Though historic for its stylistic economy and sexual audacity (it reaches its peak in an act of fetishism), and extraordinary in the lavish color and atmosphere of its designs by Leon Bakst, it is seldom seen on New York stages; the only other viewing in recent years was when Boston Ballet brought it to the Fall for Dance festival at City Center in 2009.
The response to music by Heinrich Ignaz Franz von Biber in Jorma Elo’s “Plan to B” (2004) was grossly exaggerated, especially in terms of dynamics, as if answering Baroque grace with kung fu intensity. (The women did not perform on point.) Even so, it made its six dancers individually arresting; you could understand the ovation they won.
Finally, Jiri Kylian’s “Bella Figura” (1995) was a deranged, pretentious but harmless array of assorted theatrics. Its effects included, at various points, two effigies of naked people suspended above the stage, curtains rising and falling, taped music by five different composers (from different centuries), bare-breasted women wearing scarlet crinolines, and flames rising from caldrons on either side of the stage. I almost wish the nine dancers had not done it so well; its stage world makes humans look like mere small fry.
The Boston dancers largely rose handsomely to the challenge of “Symphony in Three Movements,” with especially fine dancing from Ms. Kuranaga and Jeffrey Cirio. The Boston performance was superior to the way City Ballet danced this piece seven years ago, though it did not show all the drive and eloquence that company has now regained. I nonetheless object to the performance of Lia Cirio, a purposeful leading Boston ballerina, in the central role; in particular, the tremendous tension evident in her neck and face does much to wreck the choreography’s inscrutable grace. “Faun” cast a spell, but Altan Dugaraa’s performance, even more than in 2009, is highly exaggerated: He opens his mouth in far too many snarls, while over-softening the bas-relief style.
